preamble: Deglottalization of the alveolar ejective [tʼ] to plain [t]. The clearest direct case is Geers's law in Akkadian: a root inherited with two emphatics (reconstructed as ejectives) keeps only one, and ṭ, the least stable in the hierarchy ṣ > ḳ > ṭ, becomes plain t next to ḳ or ṣ, while Arabic, Hebrew and Geʽez cognates keep both. The rule is usually explained by the cross-linguistic ban on two ejectives in one root (Kogan 2011; MacEachern 1999). The same endpoint is reached indirectly in Maltese, Cypriot Maronite Arabic and Modern Hebrew via a pharyngealized stage (*tʼ > tˤ > t) under European contact.

examples.note: ṭ > t next to ṣ; Arabic ḍabaṭa and Hebrew ṣāḇaṭ keep both emphatics.
Hebrew qāṭān, Geʽez ḳäṭin keep ṭ.
Arabic qaṭafa, Hebrew qāṭap, Syriac qṭap.
Net *tʼ > tˤ > t; the Maltese emphatic/plain contrast was lost in late medieval times (Puech 2018).
The diphthong is a vowel trace of the lost emphatic and keeps it apart from tin 'figs' (Arabic tīn).

languageExamples.language: Biblical Hebrew to Israeli Hebrew (via tˤ)

examples.note: ṭēt merged with tav; Yemenite Hebrew keeps the emphatic.
